title: A bridge from strategy to operations
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Which of your plans has no bridge to the people who will carry it out?

A student said: in this person's case it is about eighty percent strategy and twenty percent operations. I said: I think so too. Because he looks for structures that already exist, operation-wise. When he finds operationally sound people, he can focus on strategy, because the chances of execution are high.

I then told a famous story about a great investor who bought a large soft-drink company when its market in his own country was saturated. At the first shareholder meeting he asked how many of the company's products the average consumer consumed in the United States, and then how many internationally. Everybody was stumped, because they had no international plan. They then went into worldwide franchising. That is strategy.

A student said: the power of a question. Instead of saying: you need to go international, he asked a question. I said: when you ask a question, you shift the responsibility from you to them. With a child, you ask: do you want to be organized or disorganized? You are not making the decision for him.

A student said: I think you have to quickly translate the strategy into a procedure so that you aren't the chief firefighter forever. If you are just starting out you can't just be doing strategy. You have to operationalize it, so that when the same problem shows up in two days or two months, everybody on the team knows how to do it.

I said: if you don't have a bridge between strategy and operations, you are sitting on different icebergs. Operational effectiveness is not strategy, and that is often confused. A student said: that is more tactical competence, and you do need it.

A student said: for a good strategy meeting you need a cross-section of the business, including frontline people where the rubber meets the road, who feel they can talk honestly about the barriers and shortcomings. I said: not involving operational people in strategic meetings is a huge problem.

Another said: think of a small elite military team. They don't compile the whole strategy, but they are the most tactically competent group, and each has different specialized skills, coming together on one core strategy and adapting as they go.
Who carries out your strategy, and were they in the room?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write your strategy and who will carry it out.
Write the question you could ask instead of giving an instruction.
Write who from the front line should be in your next strategy meeting.
Write the procedure that would let you stop firefighting.

check.q: What did I say happens when you ask a question?
choices: You shift the responsibility to them

check.q: What did a student say to do quickly with strategy?
What did I call not involving operational people in strategy meetings?

recap: Bridge strategy and operations. Ask questions. Bring the front line into strategy.
